claim: Responses of sensory neurons are often modeled using a weighted combination of rectified linear subunits.
source: Responses of sensory neurons are often modeled using a weighted combination of rectified linear subunits.
evidence: This is a general statement about modeling approaches in sensory neuroscience, drawing on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Subunits often cannot be measured directly.
source: Since these subunits often cannot be measured directly, a flexible method is needed to infer their properties from the responses of downstream neurons.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the experimental limitations in measuring subunits.

claim: For parasol retinal ganglion cells in macaque retina, estimated subunits partitioned the receptive field into compact regions.
source: For parasol retinal ganglion cells in macaque retina, estimated subunits partitioned the receptive field into compact regions, likely representing aggregated bipolar cell inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 2.

claim: Estimated subunits likely represent aggregated bipolar cell inputs.
source: For parasol retinal ganglion cells in macaque retina, estimated subunits partitioned the receptive field into compact regions, likely representing aggregated bipolar cell inputs.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data and inference about the biological substrate.

claim: Joint clustering revealed shared subunits between neighboring cells.
source: Joint clustering revealed shared subunits between neighboring cells, producing a parsimonious population model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Closed-loop validation revealed stronger nonlinearities in OFF cells than ON cells.
source: Closed-loop validation, using stimuli lying in the null space of the linear receptive field, revealed stronger nonlinearities in OFF cells than ON cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from null stimulus experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Responses to natural images jittered to emulate fixational eye movements were accurately predicted by the subunit model.
source: Responses to natural images, jittered to emulate fixational eye movements, were accurately predicted by the subunit model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Retinal ganglion cells are driven by nonlinear 'subunits'.
source: For example, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are known to be driven by nonlinear 'subunits' (Hochstein and Shapley, 1976), which reflect signals from presynaptic bipolar cells that are rectified at the synapse onto RGCs (Demb et al., 1999; Demb et al., 2001; Borghuis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subunits reflect signals from presynaptic bipolar cells that are rectified at the synapse onto RGCs.
source: For example, retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) are known to be driven by nonlinear 'subunits' (Hochstein and Shapley, 1976), which reflect signals from presynaptic bipolar cells that are rectified at the synapse onto RGCs (Demb et al., 1999; Demb et al., 2001; Borghuis et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The subunit computation is fundamentally nonlinear because hyperpolarization of one bipolar cell input does not cancel depolarization of another.
source: This subunit computation is fundamentally nonlinear because hyperpolarization of one bipolar cell input does not cancel depolarization of another.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known properties of neural computation.

claim: The subunit architecture endows RGCs with sensitivity to finer spatial detail than would arise from a linear receptive field.
source: The subunit architecture endows RGCs with sensitivity to finer spatial detail than would arise from a linear receptive field (Hochstein and Shapley, 1976; Demb et al., 2001;; Baccus et al., 2008; Crook et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2012) and has been implicated in the processing of visual features like object motion and looming (Olveczky et al., 2007; Münch et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subunit architecture has been implicated in the processing of visual features like object motion and looming.
source: The subunit architecture endows RGCs with sensitivity to finer spatial detail than would arise from a linear receptive field (Hochstein and Shapley, 1976; Demb et al., 2001;; Baccus et al., 2008; Crook et al., 2008; Schwartz et al., 2012) and has been implicated in the processing of visual features like object motion and looming (Olveczky et al., 2007; Münch et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Complex cells in primary visual cortex are thought to perform subunit computations on simple cell inputs, producing invariance to the spatial location of a stimulus.
source: As another example, complex cells in primary visual cortex are thought to perform subunit computations on simple cell inputs, producing invariance to the spatial location of a stimulus.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in visual neuroscience.

claim: Subunits appear to be a common computational motif in the brain.
source: Indeed, subunits appear to be a common computational motif in the brain, and inferring their functional properties from neural recordings requires the development of effective estimation methods.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in neuroscience.

claim: No widely accepted general computational tools exist for inferring the structure of nonlinear subunits providing inputs to a neuron.
source: However, no widely accepted general computational tools exist for inferring the structure of nonlinear subunits providing inputs to a neuron, such as their individual sizes, shapes, and spatial arrangement.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on knowledge of existing methods.

claim: The method was derived as a maximum likelihood procedure for estimating subunit model parameters.
source: The method was derived as a maximum likelihood procedure for estimating subunit model parameters and took the form of a spike-triggered clustering algorithm.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach developed in the manuscript.

claim: The method took the form of a spike-triggered clustering algorithm.
source: The method was derived as a maximum likelihood procedure for estimating subunit model parameters and took the form of a spike-triggered clustering algorithm.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach developed in the manuscript.

claim: The method provided a natural generalization of spike-triggered averaging.
source: As such, it provided a natural generalization of spike-triggered averaging, which is widely used to estimate linear receptive fields because of its conceptual simplicity, robustness, and straightforward interpretation.
evidence: This is an inference about the relationship between the new method and existing methods.

claim: Spike-triggered averaging is widely used to estimate linear receptive fields because of its conceptual simplicity, robustness, and straightforward interpretation.
source: As such, it provided a natural generalization of spike-triggered averaging, which is widely used to estimate linear receptive fields because of its conceptual simplicity, robustness, and straightforward interpretation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about spike-triggered averaging.

claim: The new method revealed a gradual partitioning of receptive fields with a hierarchical organization of spatially localized and regularly spaced subunits in populations of recorded parasol RGCs in macaque retina.
source: In populations of recorded parasol RGCs in macaque retina, the new method revealed a gradual partitioning of receptive fields with a hierarchical organization of spatially localized and regularly spaced subunits, consistent with the input from a mosaic of bipolar cells, and generalized naturally and parsimoniously to a population of cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The hierarchical organization of subunits is consistent with the input from a mosaic of bipolar cells.
source: In populations of recorded parasol RGCs in macaque retina, the new method revealed a gradual partitioning of receptive fields with a hierarchical organization of spatially localized and regularly spaced subunits, consistent with the input from a mosaic of bipolar cells, and generalized naturally and parsimoniously to a population of cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and known biology.

claim: The technique optimized a simple and explicit model of neural response.
source: Unlike other approaches, the technique optimized a simple and explicit model of neural response, required no assumptions about the spatio-temporal properties of subunits, and was validated on an extensive data set.
evidence: This describes a property of the method developed in the manuscript.

claim: The technique required no assumptions about the spatio-temporal properties of subunits.
source: Unlike other approaches, the technique optimized a simple and explicit model of neural response, required no assumptions about the spatio-temporal properties of subunits, and was validated on an extensive data set.
evidence: This describes a property of the method developed in the manuscript.

claim: The structure of the model permitted prior information, such as spatial locality, to be incorporated naturally in cases of limited data.
source: The structure of the model permitted prior information, such as spatial locality, to be incorporated naturally in cases of limited data.
evidence: This describes a property of the method developed in the manuscript, demonstrated in Figure 3.

claim: A novel closed-loop 'null' stimulus revealed that the subunit model was substantially more accurate than a linear model in explaining RGC responses.
source: A novel closed-loop 'null' stimulus revealed that the subunit model was substantially more accurate than a linear model in explaining RGC responses, a finding that also extended to natural stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The finding that the subunit model was more accurate than a linear model also extended to natural stimuli.
source: A novel closed-loop 'null' stimulus revealed that the subunit model was substantially more accurate than a linear model in explaining RGC responses, a finding that also extended to natural stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Responses to null stimuli were stronger in OFF parasol cells than ON parasol cells.
source: Responses to null stimuli were stronger in OFF parasol cells than ON parasol cells, consistent with their stronger nonlinear responses (Demb et al., 2001; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous research.

claim: OFF parasol cells have stronger nonlinear responses than ON parasol cells.
source: Responses to null stimuli were stronger in OFF parasol cells than ON parasol cells, consistent with their stronger nonlinear responses (Demb et al., 2001; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Turner and Rieke, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Application of the estimation method to complex cells in primary visual cortex revealed subunits with expected spatiotemporal structure.
source: Application of the estimation method to complex cells in primary visual cortex revealed subunits with expected spatiotemporal structure, demonstrating that the approach generalizes to other experimental contexts and neural circuits.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The approach generalizes to other experimental contexts and neural circuits.
source: Application of the estimation method to complex cells in primary visual cortex revealed subunits with expected spatiotemporal structure, demonstrating that the approach generalizes to other experimental contexts and neural circuits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the successful application to V1 data.

claim: In the first LN stage, visual inputs over space and recent time are weighted and summed by linear subunit filters, followed by an exponential nonlinearity.
source: In the first LN stage, visual inputs over space and recent time are weighted and summed by linear subunit filters, followed by an exponential nonlinearity.
evidence: This describes the structure of the model used in the manuscript.

claim: In the second LN stage, the subunit outputs are weighted by non-negative scalars, summed, and passed through a final output nonlinearity.
source: In the second LN stage, the subunit outputs are weighted by non-negative scalars, summed, and passed through a final output nonlinearity.
evidence: This describes the structure of the model used in the manuscript.

claim: The model yields the neuron's firing rate, which drives a Poisson spike generator.
source: This yields the neuron's firing rate, which drives a Poisson spike generator.
evidence: This describes the structure of the model used in the manuscript.

claim: Spike-triggered clustering is effective because stimuli that produce spikes will typically fall into distinct categories based on which subunit(s) they activate.
source: Intuitively, clustering is effective because stimuli that produce spikes will typically fall into distinct categories based on which subunit(s) they activate.
evidence: This is an inference about why the method works.

claim: Simulations with a RGC model show that the spike-triggered clustering procedure yields accurate estimates of model parameters when sufficient data are available.
source: Simulations with a RGC model show that this procedure yields accurate estimates of model parameters when sufficient data are available (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Setting N = 1 yielded a single subunit with a receptive field essentially identical to the STA.
source: As expected, setting N = 1 yielded a single subunit with a receptive field essentially identical to the STA, i.e. the spatial filter of a LN model.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A model with two subunits partitioned the receptive field into spatially localized regions.
source: Interestingly, a model with two subunits partitioned this receptive field into spatially localized regions (Figure 2A, second row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fitting the model with additional subunits typically caused one of the subunits from the preceding fit to be partitioned further, while other subunits were largely unchanged.
source: Fitting the model with additional subunits (Figure 2A, subsequent rows) typically caused one of the subunits from the preceding fit to be partitioned further, while other subunits were largely unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The number of model parameters increases with N, and thus the estimation accuracy decreases, with estimated subunits becoming noisier and exhibiting larger overlap.
source: However, the number of model parameters increases with N, and thus the estimation accuracy decreases, with estimated subunits becoming noisier and exhibiting larger overlap (Figure 2A, last row).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The typical optimum number of subunits for OFF parasol cells in the recorded data was 4–6 subunits.
source: The typical optimum for OFF parasol cells in the recorded data was 4–6 subunits (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: One or two subunits provided the optimum fit for 48% of ON parasol cells.
source: Since the ON parasol cells had a smaller optimum number of subunits (one or two subunits provided the optimum fit for 48% of ON parasol cells, while this held for only 3% of OFF parasol cells) and exhibited much smaller increases in likelihood of the subunit model compared to a LN model (not shown), subsequent analysis focuses only on the OFF parasol cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: One or two subunits provided the optimum fit for only 3% of OFF parasol cells.
source: Since the ON parasol cells had a smaller optimum number of subunits (one or two subunits provided the optimum fit for 48% of ON parasol cells, while this held for only 3% of OFF parasol cells) and exhibited much smaller increases in likelihood of the subunit model compared to a LN model (not shown), subsequent analysis focuses only on the OFF parasol cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: A model with multiple subunits frequently explained ON parasol data more accurately than a model with one subunit (three or more subunits for 52% of cells).
source: Note, however, that a model with multiple subunits frequently explained ON parasol data more accurately than a model with one subunit (three or more subunits for 52% of cells), implying that ON parasol cells do have spatial nonlinearities.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: ON parasol cells do have spatial nonlinearities.
source: Note, however, that a model with multiple subunits frequently explained ON parasol data more accurately than a model with one subunit (three or more subunits for 52% of cells), implying that ON parasol cells do have spatial nonlinearities.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: The estimated subunits were larger and fewer in number than expected from the size and number of bipolar cells providing input to parasol RGCs at the eccentricities recorded.
source: The estimated subunits were larger and fewer in number than expected from the size and number of bipolar cells providing input to parasol RGCs at the eccentricities recorded (Jacoby et al., 2000; Schwartz and Rieke, 2011; Tsukamoto and Omi, 2015).
evidence: This is based on comparison with cited literature.

claim: Estimated subunits were compact in space.
source: First, estimated subunits were compact in space as shown in Figure 2A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and quantified in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Compared to permuted subunits, the estimated subunits had substantially lower MSE.
source: Compared to the permuted subunits, the estimated subunits had substantially lower MSE (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: The subunits 'tiled' the RGC receptive field, in that they covered it with minimal gaps and modest overlap.
source: Second, the subunits 'tiled' the RGC receptive field, in that they covered it with minimal gaps and modest overlap.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: On average, the neighboring subunits for a given cell were separated by ∼ 1.5 times their width, with relatively little variation.
source: This was quantified by noting that on average, the neighboring subunits for a given cell were separated by ∼ 1.5 times their width, with relatively little variation (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: A natural interpretation of subunits observed with coarse stimulation is that they correspond to aggregates of neighboring bipolar cells.
source: Given these observations, a natural interpretation of subunits observed with coarse stimulation is that they correspond to aggregates of neighboring bipolar cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observations.

claim: For data simulated using coarse pixelated stimuli matched to those used in the experiments, the estimated subunits were fewer and larger than the bipolar cells, with each subunit representing an aggregate of several bipolar cells.
source: For data simulated using coarse pixelated stimuli matched to those used in the experiments, the estimated subunits were fewer and larger than the bipolar cells, with each subunit representing an aggregate of several bipolar cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The recovered subunits from simulations exhibited spatial locality and tiling, as in the data.
source: The recovered subunits also exhibited spatial locality and tiling, as in the data.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher resolution stimuli led to worse subunit estimates, even when all the recorded data (97 min) were used.
source: Higher resolution stimuli led to worse subunit estimates, even when all the recorded data (97 min) were used (Figure 3A, top row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: For coarse resolution stimuli, using only 10% of the recorded data led to noisy subunit estimates compared to the estimates obtained with 81% of the data.
source: For coarse resolution stimuli, using only 10% of the recorded data led to noisy subunit estimates (Figure 3B, top row) compared to the estimates obtained with 81% of the data (24 min, Figure 3B, last row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both L1 and LNL1 priors produced spatially localized subunits in the case of coarse resolution data.
source: In the case of the coarse resolution data, both L1 and LNL1 priors produced spatially localized subunits (Figure 3B, middle rows) whose locations matched the location of the subunits estimated using more data without regularization (Figure 3B, last row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The proposed prior leads to efficient estimates without introducing significant biases.
source: This suggests that the proposed prior leads to efficient estimates without introducing significant biases.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Relative to L1 regularization, LNL1 regularization yielded fewer apparent noise pixels in the background and a larger optimum number of subunits.
source: Relative to L1 regularization, LNL1 regularization yielded fewer apparent noise pixels in the background (Figure 3B, middle rows) and a larger optimum number of subunits (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: LNL1 regularization resulted in more accurate response prediction than L1 regularization.
source: This improvement in spatial locality is reflected in more accurate response prediction with LNL1 regularization (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the case of high dimensional stimuli, both L1 and LNL1 priors were successful in estimating compact subunits.
source: In the case of high dimensional stimuli (Figure 3A, top row), both L1 and LNL1 priors were successful in estimating compact subunits (Figure 3A, middle rows) and matched the location of subunits obtained with a coarser stimulus (Figure 3A, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The LNL1 prior led to subunit estimates with fewer spurious pixels compared to the L1 prior.
source: The LNL1 prior also led to subunit estimates with fewer spurious pixels compared to the L1 prior.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: LNL1 had a much smaller effect on estimated subunit size than L1.
source: Note that although these spurious pixels can also be suppressed by using a larger weight on the L1 prior, this also yielded smaller subunit size, which produced less accurate response predictions, while LNL1 had a much smaller effect on estimated subunit size (not shown).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: In both conditions of limited data examined, the novel LNL1 prior yielded spatially localized subunits, fewer spurious pixels, and a net improvement in response prediction accuracy.
source: Hence, in both the conditions of limited data examined, the novel LNL1 prior yielded spatially localized subunits, fewer spurious pixels, and a net improvement in response prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neighboring OFF parasol cells have partially overlapping receptive fields.
source: Since neighboring OFF parasol cells have partially overlapping receptive fields (Gauthier et al., 2009), and sample a mosaic of bipolar cells, neighboring cells would be expected to receive input from common subunits.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Neighboring cells would be expected to receive input from common subunits.
source: Since neighboring OFF parasol cells have partially overlapping receptive fields (Gauthier et al., 2009), and sample a mosaic of bipolar cells, neighboring cells would be expected to receive input from common subunits.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known biology.

claim: In mosaics of recorded OFF parasol cells, estimated subunits of different cells were frequently closer than the typical nearest-neighbor subunit distances obtained from single-cell data.
source: Indeed, in mosaics (lattices) of recorded OFF parasol cells, estimated subunits of different cells were frequently closer than the typical nearest-neighbor subunit distances obtained from single-cell data.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In one data set, the fraction of subunits from different cells closer than 1SD of a Gaussian fit was 14%, substantially higher than the predicted value of 9% based on the separation of subunits within a cell.
source: For example, in one data set, the fraction of subunits from different cells closer than 1SD of a Gaussian fit was 14%, substantially higher than the predicted value of 9% based on the separation of subunits within a cell (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 2F.

claim: Closely-spaced subunits from different cells correspond to single subunits shared by neighboring RGCs.
source: Examination of the mosaic suggests that these closely-spaced subunits correspond to single subunits shared by neighboring RGCs (Figure 4A), that is, that they reflect a shared biological substrate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A joint model with 12 subunits achieved similar test log-likelihood as a model with 15 subunits estimated separately for each cell.
source: Then, a joint model with 12 subunits was fitted. Similar test log-likelihood was observed using the joint model, which effectively reduced model complexity by three subunits (Figure 4E, horizontal line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Pairs of overlapping subunits from neighboring cells in separate fits were replaced with one shared subunit in the joint model.
source: Examination of the subunit locations revealed that pairs of overlapping subunits from neighboring cells in separate fits were replaced with one shared subunit in the joint model (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: A joint model with 15 subunits showed a higher prediction accuracy than a model in which the 15 subunits were estimated separately.
source: Also, a joint model with 15 subunits showed a higher prediction accuracy than a model in which the 15 subunits were estimated separately (Figure 4E, vertical line).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Joint fitting provided more accurate predictions than separate fits, when using a large total number of subunits (>12).
source: Joint fitting provided more accurate predictions than separate fits, when using a large total number of subunits (>12).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For a smaller number of subunits, a horizontal shift in the observed likelihood curves revealed the reduction in the number of subunits that was obtained with joint estimation, without a reduction in prediction accuracy.
source: For a smaller number of subunits, a horizontal shift in the observed likelihood curves revealed the reduction in the number of subunits that was obtained with joint estimation, without a reduction in prediction accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Jointly estimating a common collection of subunits for nearby cells resulted in a more parsimonious explanation of population responses.
source: In sum, jointly estimating a common collection of subunits for nearby cells resulted in a more parsimonious explanation of population responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A null stimulus orthogonal to the RF can be computed by subtracting a vector with the same RF projection from the original stimulus.
source: Thus, a null stimulus orthogonal to the RF can be computed by subtracting a vector with the same RF projection from the original stimulus (Figure 5B).
evidence: This describes the method for constructing null stimuli.

claim: The resulting null stimulus is the closest stimulus to the original white noise stimulus that yields zero response in a LN neuron.
source: Given these constraints, the resulting stimulus is the closest stimulus to the original white noise stimulus that yields zero response in a LN neuron.
evidence: This describes the method for constructing null stimuli.

claim: RGC firing rates showed a substantial modulation for both white noise and the null stimulus that was highly reproducible across repeats.
source: RGC firing rates showed a substantial modulation for both white noise and the null stimulus that was highly reproducible across repeats (Figure 5C,D), inconsistent with linear integration by the RGC over its RF.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The substantial modulation of RGC firing rates by null stimuli is inconsistent with linear integration by the RGC over its RF.
source: RGC firing rates showed a substantial modulation for both white noise and the null stimulus that was highly reproducible across repeats (Figure 5C,D), inconsistent with linear integration by the RGC over its RF.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: The null stimulus modulated OFF parasol cells more strongly than ON parasol cells.
source: Note that the null stimulus modulated OFF parasol cells more strongly than ON parasol cells, consistent with previous results obtained with white noise and natural scene stimuli (Demb et al., 2001; Chichilnisky and Kalmar, 2002; Turner and Rieke, 2016); henceforth, analysis is focused on OFF parasol cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and citations to previous research.

claim: The subunit model substantially captured response nonlinearities revealed by the null stimulus.
source: The subunit model substantially captured response nonlinearities revealed by the null stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The single subunit (LN) model failed to capture responses to the held-out null stimulus.
source: As expected, the single subunit (LN) model failed to capture responses to the held-out null stimulus (Figure 6A, second row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: As the number of subunits was increased, model performance progressively increased.
source: As the number of subunits was increased, model performance progressively increased (Figure 6A, subsequent rows).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The single subunit model failed for null stimuli, with prediction accuracy near 0 (mean accuracy : 0.02, 0.12, 0.03 for three retinas).
source: The single subunit model failed, with prediction accuracy near 0 (mean accuracy : 0.02, 0.12, 0.03 for three retinas).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The prediction accuracy for null stimuli gradually increased with the addition of more subunits, saturating at roughly 4–6 subunits.
source: The prediction accuracy gradually increased with the addition of more subunits, saturating at roughly 4–6 subunits (Figure 6B, red).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The addition of subunits showed marginal improvements for white noise stimuli of the same duration.
source: In contrast, the addition of subunits showed marginal improvements for white noise stimuli of the same duration (Figure 6B, black), despite being measurable with longer stimuli (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 2B.

claim: The response nonlinearities captured by the subunit model are more efficiently exposed by the null stimulus.
source: Thus, the response nonlinearities captured by the subunit model are more efficiently exposed by the null stimulus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Responses to natural stimuli showed a distinct structure, with strong periods of firing or silence immediately following saccades and less frequent firing elicited by image jitter.
source: Responses to natural stimuli showed a distinct structure, with strong periods of firing or silence immediately following saccades and less frequent firing elicited by image jitter (Heitman et al., 2016, Figure 7A black raster).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and a citation to previous research.

claim: The distinct structure of responses to natural stimuli was progressively better captured by the model as the number of subunits increased.
source: This structure was progressively better captured by the model as the number of subunits increased, as shown by the rasters for an OFF parasol cell in Figure 7A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Some of the firing events could not be captured even with a large number of subunits.
source: However, some of the firing events could not be captured even with a large number of subunits, suggesting that models with additional mechanisms such as gain control (Heeger, 1992; Carandini and Heeger, 2012) or nonlinear interactions between subunits (Kuo et al., 2016; Manookin et al., 2018) may be required to describe natural scene responses more completely.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Models with additional mechanisms such as gain control or nonlinear interactions between subunits may be required to describe natural scene responses more completely.
source: However, some of the firing events could not be captured even with a large number of subunits, suggesting that models with additional mechanisms such as gain control (Heeger, 1992; Carandini and Heeger, 2012) or nonlinear interactions between subunits (Kuo et al., 2016; Manookin et al., 2018) may be required to describe natural scene responses more completely.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental data and citations to previous research.

claim: Addition of subunits produced greater prediction improvements for responses elicited by image jitter compared to those elicited immediately following simulated saccades.
source: Interestingly, further examination revealed that addition of subunits produced greater prediction improvements for responses elicited by image jitter compared to those elicited immediately following simulated saccades (< 250 ms) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Changes in luminance are usually more spatially uniform at saccades, resulting in more linear signaling by RGCs.
source: This could be explained by the fact that changes in luminance are usually more spatially uniform at saccades, resulting in more linear signaling by RGCs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data.

claim: After temporally filtering the visual stimulus, there were fewer stimulus samples in the null space of the receptive field (90 degrees) during saccades than between saccades.
source: Indeed, after temporally filtering the visual stimulus, there were fewer stimulus samples in the null space of the receptive field (90 degrees) during saccades than between saccades (Figure 7C), and the subunit model provided a more accurate explanation of responses to stimuli in the null space (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The subunit model provided a more accurate explanation of responses to stimuli in the null space.
source: Indeed, after temporally filtering the visual stimulus, there were fewer stimulus samples in the null space of the receptive field (90 degrees) during saccades than between saccades (Figure 7C), and the subunit model provided a more accurate explanation of responses to stimuli in the null space (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Spatial non-linearities contribute to explaining responses to natural stimuli, especially those elicited by jittering images.
source: Thus, these results indicate that spatial non-linearities contribute to explaining responses to natural stimuli, especially those elicited by jittering images.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The estimated subunits from V1 neurons showed oriented spatio-temporal structure similar to that observed with other methods.
source: The estimated subunits showed oriented spatio-temporal structure similar to that observed with other methods that imposed more restrictions (Rust et al., 2005; Vintch et al., 2015) (because of this similarity, additional priors on the filters were not explored).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and citations to previous research.

claim: Increasing the number of subunits in V1 neurons typically caused one of the subunits from the preceding fits to be partitioned into two, while other subunits were largely unchanged.
source: Increasing the number of subunits typically caused one of the subunits from the preceding fits to be partitioned into two, while other subunits were largely unchanged (Figure 8); that is, a hierarchical structure similar to that observed in RGCs (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The number of cross-validated subunits for the complex cell (N = 8) was greater than for the simple cell (N = 4).
source: The number of cross-validated subunits for the complex cell (N = 8) was greater than for the simple cell (N = 4), consistent with previous work (Rust et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8 and a citation to previous research.

claim: All subunits for a given V1 cell had similar structure in space and time, but were approximately translated relative to each other.
source: All subunits for a given cell had similar structure in space and time, but were approximately translated relative to each other, consistent with the similar frequency spectrum (Figure 8A,B, bottom row).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: For the complex cell, the translational structure is consistent with the hypothesis that it receives inputs from multiple simple cells at different locations.
source: For the complex cell, this is consistent with the hypothesis that it receives inputs from multiple simple cells at different locations (Hubel and Wiesel, 1962; Adelson and Bergen, 1985; Vintch et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data and citations to previous research.

claim: The method presented here extends to V1 data, producing subunit estimates that are not constrained by assumptions of orthogonality or convolutional structure.
source: Thus, the method presented here extends to V1 data, producing subunit estimates that are not constrained by assumptions of orthogonality (Rust et al., 2005) or convolutional structure (Vintch et al., 2015), yet broadly resembling the results of previous work (see Discussion and Figure 10 for a detailed comparison).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data shown in Figure 8 and comparison to previous work.

claim: For a realistic amount of data, the SNMF approach often produced mixtures of underlying subunits, while the spike-triggered clustering approach produced unique and separate subunits.
source: In these conditions, recovery of subunits revealed two trends. First, for a realistic amount of data, the SNMF approach often produced mixtures of underlying subunits, while the spike-triggered clustering approach produced unique and separate subunits (see Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The spatial structure of extracted subunit was substantially more variable using SNMF across different initializations.
source: Second, the spatial structure of extracted subunit was substantially more variable using SNMF across different initializations.
evidence: This is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 9.

claim: In simulated conditions, the spike-triggered clustering method produces more consistent and accurate estimates of subunit spatial structure than SNMF.
source: These results indicate that, at least in these simulated conditions, the spike-triggered clustering method produces more consistent and accurate estimates of subunit spatial structure than SNMF.
evidence: This is a summary of the simulation data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The convolutional model was substantially more efficient, exhibiting lower prediction error for limited training data.
source: As expected, the convolutional model was substantially more efficient, exhibiting lower prediction error for limited training data.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: For longer durations of training data (within the range of typical experiments), the unconstrained model exhibited lower error.
source: However, for longer durations of training data (within the range of typical experiments), the unconstrained model exhibited lower error (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The spatial location and resulting layout of subunits obtained from the convolutional and spike-triggered clustering methods were similar.
source: The spatial location and resulting layout of subunits obtained from the two methods were similar (Figure 10B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: Spike-triggered clustering captured the deviations from a purely convolutional structure, leading to improved performance.
source: However, spike-triggered clustering captured the deviations from a purely convolutional structure, leading to improved performance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The nearly identical power spectra of the subunits estimated using spike-triggered clustering suggested nearly convolutional structure, without explicitly enforcing this constraint.
source: Note that the nearly identical power spectra (Figure 8) of the subunits estimated using spike-triggered clustering suggested nearly convolutional structure, without explicitly enforcing this constraint.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Replacing the exponential nonlinearity with a quadratic nonlinearity provided more accurate fits for both models in V1 neurons.
source: Note that further improvement in both approaches could potentially be achieved with modifications. For example in the V1 neurons, replacing the exponential nonlinearity with a quadratic nonlinearity (as in Vintch et al., 2015) provided more accurate fits for both models, but the performance of spike-triggered clustering was still superior when more data were available (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: The performance of spike-triggered clustering was still superior to the convolutional model when more data were available, even with a quadratic nonlinearity.
source: Note that further improvement in both approaches could potentially be achieved with modifications. For example in the V1 neurons, replacing the exponential nonlinearity with a quadratic nonlinearity (as in Vintch et al., 2015) provided more accurate fits for both models, but the performance of spike-triggered clustering was still superior when more data were available (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.
